title: The Insider's Illusion
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] There is a particular vanity in believing you have found the real version of a city, as though authenticity were a hidden room only you had discovered.
Narrator: I used to pride myself on avoiding anywhere mentioned in a guidebook, as if obscurity were itself a form of virtue.
Narrator: [carefully] It took me embarrassingly long to notice the flaw in that logic: the moment a place becomes known for being undiscovered, it has already stopped being so.
Narrator: Every hidden gem I ever found had, of course, been found by someone else first, usually several someones, all quietly congratulating themselves on the same discovery.
Narrator: [reflective] What I was really chasing wasn't authenticity at all, but the feeling of being exempt from the crowd I was, in every practical sense, still part of.
Narrator: I don't think this impulse is shameful exactly, only a little self-deceiving, a way of dressing ordinary tourism in the costume of pilgrimage.
Narrator: [honestly] The turn for me came at a market stall run by a woman who had clearly performed the same authentic transaction a thousand times that week alone.
Narrator: She wasn't unwelcoming, just tired, and her performance of hospitality was as calculated, and as reasonable, as any transaction anywhere else.
Narrator: [gently] I realized authenticity was never really a property of places, but a demand tourists place on people, one that flattens their labour into scenery.
Narrator: Once I stopped hunting for the real version of anywhere, travel got considerably less exhausting, and, oddly, rather more interesting.
Narrator: [calmly] I began asking what a place actually needed from its visitors, rather than what it might be persuaded to perform for them.
Narrator: It's a smaller, less flattering kind of travel, admittedly, one without the satisfaction of having discovered anything remarkable at all.
Narrator: [encouraging] But it leaves less residue behind, both for the place itself and for whatever remains of my own self-regard.
Narrator: These days I visit the places every guidebook already lists, and simply try to be a decent, unremarkable guest while I'm there.
Narrator: [seriously] That, it turns out, is a far harder standard to meet than finding somewhere no one else has ever been.

quiz.question: What flaw does the narrator eventually notice in her earlier approach to travel?
options: The moment a place becomes known as undiscovered, it has already stopped being so
Guidebooks were always wrong
Obscure places were too expensive
She was too shy to explore alone
quiz.explanation: She realizes that a place's undiscovered reputation collapses the instant it becomes known for being undiscovered.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say about the woman at the market stall?
options: She refused to serve tourists
Her performance of hospitality was as calculated, and as reasonable, as any transaction elsewhere
She was rude to the narrator
She gave the narrator a discount
quiz.explanation: The narrator observes that the woman's hospitality was a tired, calculated performance, no different from any other transaction.

quiz.question: What does the narrator conclude authenticity actually is?
options: A fixed property of certain places
Something only found in guidebooks
A demand tourists place on people, flattening their labour into scenery
An outdated concept with no real meaning
quiz.explanation: She concludes authenticity is a demand placed on people rather than a quality inherent to places.

quiz.question: How does the narrator describe her travel now compared to before?
options: Smaller and less flattering, without the satisfaction of discovering something remarkable
Identical to how it always was
More expensive and elaborate
Focused entirely on famous landmarks only
quiz.explanation: She calls her current approach smaller and less flattering, lacking the old thrill of discovery.

quiz.question: What is the narrator's new standard for travel?
options: Being a decent, unremarkable guest at well-known places
Finding places no one else has visited
Avoiding all guidebook locations
Photographing empty streets
quiz.explanation: She now aims simply to be a decent, unremarkable guest at places already listed in every guidebook.

quiz.question: What false confidence is exposed by the market-stall encounter?
options: Authenticity is a demand visitors place on workers, not a hidden property of places.
Finding an unknown place makes a traveller exempt from ordinary tourism.
A tired market seller revealed the labour behind a tourist’s desired experience.
The narrator replaces personal distinction with attention to what a place needs.
